lawyer:
Moazzem Hossain with Nurul Islam Chowdhury and Ashanul Kabir ------ For the Appellant.

full_judgment:
3. The suit is barred by limitation. The plaintiff Bank had taken signatures of the defendant Company's Managing Director Mr AH Mahmood in 1969 and those blank forms have been subsequently filled up and fabricated by the plaintiff Bank in 1982 and 1983. Taking of signatures on blank forms and papers is illegal and those documents are of no legal effect. The transaction in the defendant's account was closed since April, 1976. Thereafter there was no transaction in the account. The accrual of interest was also stopped in the account with effect from 3-10-74. In order to bring the suit within limitation the plaintiff has falsely introduced the story in the plaint that the defendant Company executed on 18-2-82 fresh Pro-note, Revival letter, Letter of Continuity and on 18-2-82 also deposited Title Deed No. 4103 dated 25-7-66 under a Memo of deposit of title deed which is baseless. In the letter dated 5-1-82 (Exhibit 3) the defendant merely requested the management of the Pubali Bank to waive the total interest without admitting any liability. In his letter Exhibit 3 dated 5-1-82 the defendant Company requested the plaintiff Bank for giving certain business facilities, such as fixing a credit limit for Taka twenty five lacs, to allow the defendant to open letters of credit at nil margin, etc. which were obviously not accepted by the Bank. The story of executing charge security documents on 13-2-82 is false and concocted. The title deed was handed over to the Bank long ago. The story of deposit of Title Deed in 1982 is concocted. The Pro-note and Revival Letter being insufficiently stamped is inadmissible in evidence, null and void, inoperative and without any legal effect. The suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 2. Is the suit barred by limitation? 

 6. Syed Moazzem Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant appellant submits that it will appear from the Ledger Account No. 3555 Exhibit 2 that after 22 April 1976 the defendant Company made no transaction with the plaintiff Bank, that the defendant Company by its letter Exhibit A(7) dated 30-7-76 to the plaintiff Bank requested the plaintiff to waive the outstanding liability (interest) of Taka 3,83,658.48 in view of his great financial loss and helpless condition, that the outstanding debt balance against the defendant Company was at that time Taka 3,83,658.24 which became barred by limitation in 1979 as no suit was filed within three years from that date of 1976 and that thereafter also the defendant Company did not operate the account at any time till date. The plaintiff Bank by its letter Exhibit A dated 14 July 1978 asked the defendant Company to arrange to pay the said long outstanding overdraft balance. The learned Advocate for the defendant appellant submits that defendant's letter dated 5-1-82 (Exhibit, 3) was in continuation of his previous representations regarding the total waiver of the outstanding interest amount of Taka 3,83,658.34 and for sanctioning a credit limit for Taka 25,00,000 (Taka twenty five lacs) for helping him in the matter of import and export business and that in the said letter Exhibit 3 dated 5-1-82 the defendant appellant made no promise to pay the time barred debt. He further submits that the pro-note Exhibit 4, Revival Letter Exhibit 5, Letter of Continuity Exhibit 6 and Memorandum of Deposit of Title Deeds Exhibit 7 were signed by the defendant in blank, but those have been later on filled in by inserting the promise to pay the amount of Taka three lacs eighty three thousand six hundred fifty eight and paisa twenty four only with date 18-3-82 in Exhibit 4, Exhibit 5 and Exhibit 7 and by putting the date 18-3-83 in the Letter of Continuity Exhibit 6. He further submits that even if the promissory note Exhibit 4 is accepted as properly written and duly signed on 18-3-82, it is not admissible in evidence due to insufficiency of stamp because of the provision of section 35 of the Stamp Act as it bears only revenue stamp of paisa fifty in place of two taka and as such by the said promissory note Exhibit 4 the time barred debt cannot be revived within the meaning of section 25(3) of the Contract Act. He further submits that therefore the connected Revival Letter Exhibit 5 and the Letter of Continuity Exhibit 6 arising from Promissory Note Exhibit 4 have also no legal effect for the purpose of section 25 (3) of the Contract Act. 

 9. There is no dispute regarding the fact that the defendant appellant was operating his Current Account No. 3555 in the Laldighi East Branch of the Eastern Mercantile Bank Ltd. from Pakistan days (i.e. from 1965). There is also no dispute regarding the fact that the Eastern Mercantile Bank Ltd (as the plaintiff's Bank name was at that time) by their letter dated 3-2-70 (Exhibit 1) sanctioned LC Limit of Taka 2,50,000 in favour of the defendant appellant against the said Current Account. From the Ledger Account Sheets Exhibit 2 it clearly appears that the amount payable by the defendant appellant to the plaintiff Bank on 22 April 1976 was Taka 3,83,658.24. There is also no dispute regarding the fact that the defendant appellant did not operate the Bank account thereafter till date. It appears that the defendant appellant started submitting petitions to the plaintiff Bank for stopping the calculation of interest on the ground that his financial condition is very bad as the market price of the imported goods are continuing to fall. He, however, prayed for waiving of interest by his letter Exhibit A (7) dated 30-7-76. Though the plaintiff Bank did not waive the interest, but apparently on humanitarian grounds stopped the calculation of any further interest on the aforesaid dues to be paid by the defendant appellant to the plaintiff Bank. The plaintiff Bank has not filed any letter to show that the defendant after sending his letter Exhibit A (7) dated 30-7-76 sent any other letter within 3 years after that date to the plaintiff Bank in this regard. Therefore the debt became barred by limitation on 30-7-1979. There is also no dispute regarding the fact that the defendant appellant wrote the letter Exhibit 3 dated 5-1-82 to the plaintiff Bank (i.e. to the Managing Director, Pubali Bank, Dilkusha Commercial Area Dhaka, through the Manager, Pubali Bank, Laldighi East Branch, Chittagong) stating as follows:— 

 "Pubali Bank, Laldighi East Branch. With reference to our overdraft Cash Credit Account with you secured by a Demand Promissory Note dated the 18-2-82 for Rs 3,83,658.24 with interest made by us in your favour We acknowledge for the purpose of section 19 of the Limitation Act (IX of 1908) and any like Limitation Law in order to preclude any question of Limitation Law that we are liable to you for payment of the said promissory note with interest and the same is to remain in force with all relative securities, agreements and obligations. 

 He further submits that an insufficiently stamped Promissory Note cannot be admitted in evidence and cannot be acted upon as an acknowledgement of debt or as an agreement promising to pay a time barred debt on demand either as it is or after being impounded and that limitation for a suit based on the original consideration cannot be saved by putting in a subsequently executed insufficiently stamped promissory note agreeing to pay a time-barred debt. He referred to the decision of a learned Single Judge in the case of Jogendra Chandra Banerjee vs Sachindar Kumar Seal, 40 CWN 399. Mr SC Das, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff respondent draws our attention to proviso (c) to section 35 of the Stamp Act (already quoted by us) and submits that Exhibits.4 to 7 which are contract or agreement executed on the same day in the same transaction and are regarding the unconditional promise to pay only the aforesaid total amount of time barred debt with interest contained all together a total stamp duty of seven Taka, each of the documents Exhibit 6 and 7 having stamp of the value of three Taka and therefore it cannot be said that it is insufficiently stamped, that this principle is laid down in proviso (c) to the said section 35 of the Stamp Act wherein it is provided that where a contract or agreement of any kind is effected in two or more letters and any one of them bears the proper stamp, the contract or agreement shall be deemed to be duly stamped and that even if the Promissory Note Exhibit 4 is taken in isolation and treated to be insufficiently stamped, it was admitted in the evidence without any objection in the trial Court and that therefore on the ground of insufficiency of stamp its admission cannot be questioned at any stage of the suit (including appeal and revision) subsequently in view of the provision of section 36 of the Stamp Act which reads as follows:— 

 15. There is no dispute regarding the fact that the debt became barred by limitation in 1979. The present suit instituted on 16-11-83 is based on a promise to pay made in writing and signed by the defendant on 18-2-82 to be charged with the said time-barred debt unconditionally on demand which comes within the ambit of section 25(3) of the Contract Act relevant portion of which reads as follows: 

 (3) it is a promise, made in writing and signed by the person to be charged therewith, or by his agent generally or specially authorised in that behalf, to pay wholly or in part a debt of which the creditor might have enforced payment but for the law for the limitation of suit. In any of these cases such an agreement is a contract. Illustration. 

 (c) A owes B Taka 1,000 but the debt barred by Limitation Act. A signs a written promises to pay B Taka 500 on account of the debt. This is a contract". 

 "But the observation (of the Privy Council) embodies a general principle which is of universal application and I respectfully follow this observation of the Privy Council (in the case of Maniram vs Seth Rupchand, 33 Indian Appeals 165 ILR 33 (Cal) 1047 (PC). Applying that observation to the facts of this case I find that unqualified acknowledgement made by the debtor is by itself a promise to pay. Therefore, this document, namely, the said letter dated 2-12-60 is an agreement as contemplated by section 25(3) of the Contract Act and gives a fresh starting point of limitation to the Bank for realisation of the debt specified in the said letter...... 

 In the instant case it is not only an unconditional acknowledgement of the debt but also unconditional promise to pay the time barred debt in writing under the signature of the defendant and therefore there is no question of its being merely an acknowledgement of the debt and Section 19 of the Limitation Act has no application in the present case as no acknowledgement of the liability to pay the amount due was made before the expiration of the period of limitation for instituting a suit for recovery of the amount due. The present case unambiguously and directly comes within the ambit of section 25(3) of the Contract Act.
